nodes.label: Discord user
nodes.summary: Opens a WebSocket for chat and a second WebSocket plus UDP for voice.

nodes.label: API (monolith)
nodes.summary: Receives writes such as sending a message and talks to the data services. The 2023 post calls it the API monolith.

nodes.label: Session process
nodes.summary: One Elixir GenServer per connected user. Subscribes to the user's guilds (about 5 on average). Up to 500,000 live sessions per VM at the time.
nodes.details: Ring lookups for session restarts were cut from ~30 s to under a second using FastGlobal (constant module data).

nodes.label: Guild process
nodes.summary: One GenServer per guild. Publishes every event to all connected sessions. Large guilds (30,000 users) fell behind: one send/2 took 30–70 µs, so one publish took 0.9–2.1 s.

nodes.label: Manifold
nodes.summary: Batches a publish: groups recipient PIDs by remote node, sends one message per node to a partitioner that spreads local delivery across cores.
nodes.details: Semaphore (an ETS counter) makes callers fail early when too many requests are outstanding, instead of a circuit breaker.

nodes.label: Member list (Rust SortedSet)
nodes.summary: Rust NIF via Rustler for a sorted set that handles hundreds of thousands of entries. Insert 0.61–3.68 µs. Lets clients receive updates only for the visible part of the list.

nodes.label: Read States service
nodes.summary: Tracks which channels and messages each user has read. Rewritten from Go to Rust to remove GC latency spikes every ~2 minutes.

nodes.label: Data services (Rust)
nodes.summary: Sit between the API monolith and the databases. Coalesce concurrent identical row requests into one query, using consistent-hash routing by channel ID.

nodes.label: ScyllaDB (messages)
nodes.summary: Messages partitioned by channel plus a time bucket, with Snowflake IDs (time-sortable). 177 Cassandra nodes became 72 ScyllaDB nodes at 9 TB each.
nodes.details: p99 reads 40–125 ms → ~15 ms. Inserts 5–70 ms → steady 5 ms. Cutover May 2022.

nodes.label: Voice discovery (etcd)
nodes.summary: Voice servers report load to etcd. The Guilds service assigns the least-utilised voice server in the region to the guild.

nodes.label: Voice server
nodes.summary: Elixir signaling component plus a C++ SFU that forwards audio and video within a channel. Client-server, not peer-to-peer. Audio over UDP, no ICE, Salsa20 encryption.
nodes.details: 850+ voice servers in 13 regions and 2.6 million+ concurrent voice users at the time (2018).

nodes.label: Gateway (sessions + guilds)
nodes.summary: The Elixir real-time tier: a session process per user, a process per guild, Manifold fan-out and the member list.
nodes.details: Grouping container: it names the units the sources describe together. The components inside it are listed in the Components view.

flows.name: Send a message to a guild

steps.caption: The client sends the message through the API.
The write goes through the Rust data services. (The posts do not show whether persisting or publishing comes first, so this order is a labelled assumption.)
Data services route by channel ID to one instance, coalesce concurrent identical reads, and talk to ScyllaDB, where the row's partition is channel plus time bucket.
The event is published to the guild process.
The guild hands the publish to Manifold instead of sending N messages itself.
Manifold groups sessions by remote node and sends one message per node, then spreads local delivery across cores.
Each session pushes the event down its WebSocket to the user.
The client requests older messages for a channel.
The request goes to the data services, which route by channel ID.
If many users ask for the same rows, only one database query is made. p99 reads dropped to ~15 ms after the move to ScyllaDB.
The client's join request reaches the Guilds service, which consults voice discovery.
Discovery assigns the least utilised voice server in the guild's region.
The client opens a second WebSocket to that server for signaling and sends audio over UDP. The SFU forwards it to others in the channel.

flows.name: A very large guild falls behind

steps.caption: An event is published to a guild process. In 2017, a large guild could take 0.9–2.1 s per publish.
Manifold groups recipient sessions by node and sends one message per node.
Each node fans out locally across cores.
Sessions push the event to their users. This is how Discord reduced the cost of fan-out.
